summary: Boar's Head light at the entrance to Petit Passage, Nova Scotia, was opened in 1864; its present white tower dates from 1957, and the Municipality of Digby took it over in 2016.

lens.note: Changed from a revolving light to 5th order dioptric light by the report for the fiscal year 1907-08

structures.note: First lighthouse, a square wooden building painted white (1881 Sailing Directions, as Lighthouse Friends quotes it). Lighthouse Friends says it was erected in 1863; Parks Canada and Islands History give 1864 as the opening.
White square tower with red upper portion (Coast Guard list gives 11.6 m). Lighthouse Friends gives 10.7 m; see notes_for_editor.

access.note: Grounds open, tower closed (Lighthouse Friends). Reached by ferry from East Ferry to Tiverton, then a paved road to a gate; if the gate is shut, a steep one-kilometre walk.

facts.agency: Municipality of the District of Digby (owner since August 2016); the Tiverton and Central Grove Historical Association manages the property

events.note: First lighthouse opened at the entrance to Petit Passage. Lighthouse Friends says it was erected in 1863 with Henry M. Ruggles as keeper.

Land of 9.97 acres sold by Simondson and Cecelia Outhouse to the federal Minister of Marine and Fisheries for $120; the deed, as Islands History describes it, notes the light was already standing (deed not seen).
Revolving light changed to a 5th order dioptric light, as the Department reported for the fiscal year 1907-08
Fog alarm with a diaphone and gasoline engines established (Lighthouse Friends); the Department's reports read here do not show the 1910 work at this station
Grounding on 7 June 1912; the master was found alone to blame
Protection work to the dwelling and repairs to the road, as the St. John agency reported
Present white square tower built, replacing the aging wooden lighthouse
Contaminated soil around the lighthouse removed and replaced with clean fill; $216,000 cleanup under the federal Contaminated Sites Action Plan (Lighthouse Friends, citing the Digby Courier)
Designated a heritage lighthouse under the Heritage Lighthouse Protection Act (Lighthouse Friends)
Municipality of Digby took ownership in August 2016
Tiverton and Central Grove Heritage Association unveiled a four-foot memorial listing the keepers

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Lighthouse Friends says erected in 1863 with Henry M. Ruggles as keeper; Parks Canada and Islands History say the first lighthouse was opened in 1864. The story uses 1864 as the year lit, and mentions the 1863 erection.
The record's 1957 date (Parks Canada record) is the present tower; the first lighthouse dates from 1864. Both dates are sourced.
The record's 18.0 m (map source) conflicts with the Coast Guard list's 28.0 m focal height. The Coast Guard list is used.

Lighthouse Friends gives 1863 for the erection; Islands History gives 1863 for the building and 1864 for the official opening; Parks Canada says erected 1864. The story uses 1864 for the opening and states the 1863 date.

Lighthouse Friends names the Saint Croix Courier; Islands History's caption above the notice gives the Yarmouth Light, 24 July 1893. The story states both; the paper is unsettled. The Digby Courier is named by Islands History only on other captioned items.

notes_for_editor: No USLHS roster exists for Canada; keepers come from Lighthouse Friends (secondary, facts only) and the Department's keepers' tables (OCR, read by column position: 'Ruggles, Frank Boars Head' is matched on the same printed line, so the check is by position). Names after about 1960 are given only as Lighthouse Friends prints them. (1) Tower height: Lighthouse Friends says 10.7 m; the Coast Guard list gives 11.6 m; the story gives the Coast Guard figure with the conflict noted. (2) The 1893 notice: Lighthouse Friends names the Saint Croix Courier; Islands History puts the death notice in a Digby Courier of 28 July 1893 and its caption above the notice reads Yarmouth Light, 24 July 1893. The newspaper was not seen; the story says only 'a notice' and cites both. (3) The Amelia link: the wreck table in the 1914 report (scan 190) gives the Boar's Head grounding of 7 June 1912 but its name column does not line up cleanly; the survey account (scan 372) names ss. Amelia stranded on Boar's Head, dated 3 July 1912. The page number of scan 372 is not confirmed (printed page not read). (4) Parks Canada says two ships were wrecked on 16 March 1911 and 1912 and names neither; the Department's 1911 casualty list read here has no 16 March Nova Scotia loss; the 16 March 1912 loss in the Department's list is the Bona Vista on Brier Island, a different station. (5) The 1920 entry (scan 95) is under a heading 'NEW BRUNSWICK' in the OCR, with the Boar's Head line in the St. John agency text; the diaphone room item in the same block was not used. (6) The Parks Canada Directory of Federal Heritage Designations page (page_hl_eng.aspx?id=14595) returned no text, and the statement was read through the Canadian Register page instead. (7) Focal height 28.0 m and range 17 nm come from the Coast Guard list by column position. (8) Chronicling America has no usable pages for this station; no Nova Scotia newspaper archive was reachable. (9) The deed of 1868 is known only through Islands History and was not seen. (10) Lighthouse Friends dates the fog alarm to 1910; the Department's 1910 reports read here do not show it at this station. Fact-check 2026-10-27 (independent checker): wreck page 1914 p. 183 (scan 190) and keeper table 1907 p. 174 (scan 183) read on the page image; the Ruggles row is confirmed. The Amelia row on the wreck page lines up with the 7 June entry, and the table lists a second Amelia for 8 August at Clark's Harbour. The survey account (scan 372) printed page is still unconfirmed. Islands History's caption order was read as caption-before-text, so the notice caption reads Yarmouth Light; the deed of 1868 was not seen.
